w: Plain Georgian brick hides the room where the United States argued itself into being. The Continental Congress founded an army here in 1775, adopted the Declaration in 1776, then returned in 1787 for the Constitution. Locals once called it simply "the greatest ornament in the town."
s: Where a nation talked itself into existence
_facts: originally the Pennsylvania State House, completed 1753
Second Continental Congress met here 1775-1781, founded Continental Army June 14 1775
Declaration of Independence adopted here July 4 1776
hosted the Constitutional Convention May-Sept 1787
designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979

w: Nicknamed "Big J," this Iowa-class battleship earned more battle stars than her three sisters and was the only US battleship to fire in the Vietnam War. She shelled Guam and Okinawa in WWII, raided Korea, then came out of mothballs twice more before a last turn off Lebanon in 1983. Now a museum ship on the Delaware.
s: The most-decorated US battleship, retired to the river
_facts: Iowa-class battleship, earned more battle stars than the other three completed Iowa-class ships
only US battleship to provide gunfire support during the Vietnam War
shelled Guam and Okinawa in WWII; raids off North Korea in Korean War
reactivated 1968 for Vietnam and again in 1980s for the 600-ship Navy program; supported 1983 Lebanon operations
decommissioned 1991, now a museum ship

w: For a few years after 1894 this was the tallest habitable building on Earth, and it's still the largest free-standing masonry structure ever built - brick, marble and limestone stacked into ornate Second Empire towers. It still runs the city: mayor's office, council chambers, three courts, one roof.
s: Tallest building of 1894, still the largest masonry one
_facts: Second Empire style, built of brick, white marble and limestone
world's largest free-standing masonry building
world's tallest habitable building on completion in 1894
National Historic Landmark 1976; National Historic Civil Engineering Landmark 2006
houses the Mayor's office, City Council chambers, and First Judicial District courts

w: Chartered for the 1876 Centennial Exposition but not finished until 1928, this hilltop museum holds over 240,000 objects - sculpture, prints, armor, decorative arts - plus satellite outposts: the Rodin Museum and the Perelman Building's costume and textile trove. Two colonial-era houses hide in the grounds too.
s: 240,000 objects, and two colonial houses in the grounds
_facts: chartered 1876 for the Centennial Exposition; main building completed 1928 on Fairmount hill
collection of over 240,000 objects across sculpture, painting, prints, armor, decorative arts
administers the Rodin Museum and the Perelman Building (prints, costume, textiles)
also administers colonial-era houses Mount Pleasant and Cedar Grove in Fairmount Park

n: First Bank of the United States
w: Chartered by Congress in 1791 as Alexander Hamilton's answer to a fledgling nation's shaky credit, this was one leg of his three-part financial overhaul, alongside a mint and excise taxes. The building went up in 1797 and still stands inside Independence National Historical Park.
s: Alexander Hamilton's first shot at a national bank
_facts: chartered by Congress Feb 25 1791, for a 20-year term
followed the Bank of North America, the nation's first de facto national bank
part of Alexander Hamilton's three-part fiscal expansion (bank, mint, excise taxes)
building completed 1797; National Historic Landmark within Independence National Historical Park

w: Dedicated during the 1926 Sesquicentennial Exposition marking 150 years since the Declaration was signed, this suspension bridge briefly held the record for the longest span in the world. It still carries traffic, cyclists, and the PATCO Speedline across the Delaware to Camden, New Jersey.
s: Once the world's longest suspension span
_facts: originally named the Delaware River Bridge, connects Philadelphia and Camden, NJ
dedicated as part of the 1926 Sesquicentennial Exposition (150th anniversary of the Declaration)
held the record for longest suspension span in the world from 1926 to 1929
carries I-676/US 30, pedestrians, cyclists, and the PATCO Speedline

w: For decades an unwritten rule held that nothing in Center City could rise above William Penn's hat atop City Hall. Developer Willard Rouse broke the pact in 1984, and despite furious opposition over the skyline, One Liberty Place went up anyway by 1987, spire and all - first domino in the race for height.
s: The tower that broke a century-old pact with William Penn
_facts: skyscraper complex: One Liberty Place (61 storeys, 945ft) and Two Liberty Place (58 storeys, 848ft), plus a mall and hotel
broke a longstanding gentlemen's agreement not to build taller than the William Penn statue on City Hall
developer Willard G. Rouse III announced plans in 1984 amid strong opposition
One Liberty Place completed 1987, Two Liberty Place 1990
